Approving every report at or above the reserve sorts agents as if their beliefs were observed, under every strictly proper score and for any belief distribution. So does a continuous rule with one corner; under strict feasibility no continuously differentiable rule does. The binding constraint is steepness, not smoothness: a slope-capped rule sorts perfectly if and only if the cap reaches the critical slope, the steepest chord of the pretending cost up to the reserve; below it the welfare loss is cubic in the shortfall. For the Brier, log and power scores, and whenever the pretending cost is convex up to the reserve, the critical slope has a closed form. The instances are AI-agent oversight and marketplace operation.
entries.title: The Endogeneity of Miscalibration: Impossibility and Escape in Scored Reporting

entries.abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.
entries.title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents

entries.abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.
entries.comment: 43 pages, including supplementary material. Zhengru Fang and Zehao Liu contributed equally. Project page: https://egowitness.github.io/ ; Code: https://github.com/egowitness/EgoWitness
entries.title: EgoWitness: Benchmarking Instance-Level Spatial Memory and Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams

entries.abstract: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.
entries.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature

entries.abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.
entries.comment: 22 pages, 3 figures. Qiming Huang, Hanze Dong, and Jipeng Zhang contributed equally
entries.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management

entries.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are a form of life is a scientifically interesting question. Under the Darwinian definition of life, it is also a practical one, because a system capable of Darwinian Evolution can adapt. We therefore test several modes in which a language model can reproduce itself: by emitting a genome that trains its offspring, by copying and mutating its own weights, and by teaching a child from its own samples. In principle, small language models can replicate and evolve: selection improves them, and they adapt to narrow niches. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model, unlike any organism, can lower its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship LLMs can write such replicators, but for a large LLM to replicate by teaching its offspring remains, for now, technically and economically infeasible.
entries.comment: About 64 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables. Under review at Artificial Life
entries.title: Self-Replicating Language Models

entries.abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/
entries.title: ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation for Interactive Game Worlds

entries.abstract: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.
entries.title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response

entries.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.
entries.comment: 22 pages, 17 figures. v2: Updated title and author notes, and added a citation in Related Work
entries.title: Controllable Chains of Thought Can Reveal Less, Even Without Evasion Training

entries.abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Reproducibility artifact linked in the manuscript
entries.title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures

entries.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become a common source of information, users may contribute less original knowledge to the public communities on which model development depends. Platforms seeking user contributions must account for privacy and effort costs and the incentive to rely on contributions from others. We study this dilemma in a threshold public-goods model with heterogeneous user costs. Under uniform per-unit subsidies, users can be paid even when aggregate contributions fall short of the improvement threshold. To address this subsidy leakage, we develop a mechanism that combines verifiable cost disclosure, personalized contribution assignments, and voluntary withdrawal. We show that rational assignment leads either to profitable provision or to no collection. Simultaneous withdrawal minimizes contribution costs when both protocols succeed, while small-first sequential withdrawal can sustain provision under a wider range of cost conditions. Numerical experiments quantify the effects on provision probability and social welfare. In an exploratory dialogue experiment, we evaluate LLM agents based on 50 anonymized American Community Survey profiles under all three mechanisms, generating 150 trajectories to compare contribution and withdrawal decisions under matched conditions. These findings clarify how assignment rules and withdrawal timing can support collective data provision while preserving user control.
entries.title: Incentivizing User Data Contributions for LLM Improvement under Withdrawal Rights

entries.abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.
entries.title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing

entries.abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FASTFarm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.
entries.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: Task offloading in End-Edge-Cloud computing enables resource-constrained User Devices (UDs) to execute computation-intensive applications with reduced latency and energy consumption. However, existing task offloading schemes generally overlook the heterogeneous privacy requirements of users, leading to inefficient privacy-aware offloading decisions. In this paper, we propose a personalized privacy-aware task offloading framework, where the privacy requirement of each task is quantified through a User-Centric Privacy (UCP) model that considers task sensitivity, user privacy preferences, and task urgency. The task offloading problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to jointly optimize the offloading ratio and the target computing server while minimizing the long-term system cost under latency, energy, and privacy constraints. To efficiently solve the resulting high-dimensional continuous optimization problem, we develop an Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (AWAC)-enhanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithm under the Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves lower average system cost, lower energy consumption, and higher task success rate than representative baselines under diverse privacy requirements.
entries.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for presentation at IEEE CloudNet 2026
entries.title: Personalized Privacy-Aware MARL Offloading in the Edge-Cloud Continuum

entries.abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.
entries.comment: 71 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project website: https://x-lance.github.io/SynthDCB/
entries.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

entries.abstract: O-RAN enables a disaggregated baseband stack with programmable functions that communicate over standardized open interfaces. The same openness that enables multi-vendor composition also expands the attack surface across logically decoupled tiers that make up the compute continuum. Among these threats, Denial-of-Service and performance-degradation attacks, which account for the majority of catalogued O-RAN threats, are particularly difficult to detect. Traditional Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) methods fail in this new regime where labelled baselines are scarce, threats evolve faster than detectors can be retrained, and the high-dimensional multivariate telemetry overwhelms monolithic inference models. To address these challenges, we present DAST, a zero-shot multi-agent framework for cross-interface anomaly detection in O-RAN that chains a three-stage VLM $\rightarrow$ LLM $\rightarrow$ VLM pipeline. DAST converts multivariate KPI streams into visual representations, scores textual per-interface descriptions against O-RAN domain knowledge, and verifies suspects on high-resolution heatmaps to output the problematic interfaces, the anomalous time intervals, an indicative O-RAN WG11-aligned operational impact rating and the decision rationale. We evaluate DAST on real network traces collected from an O-RAN testbed under representative performance degradation scenarios, achieving 0.910 F1-Score and 0.843 Accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art TSAD baselines.
entries.comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
entries.title: DAST: A VLM-LLM Framework for Cross-Interface Anomaly Detection in O-RAN

entries.abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.
entries.title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures

entries.abstract: Embedded board-level development demands extensive expertise, from component selection and device characteristics to interface configuration, driver writing, and system composition. Recently, LLM-based agents have shown strong capabilities, raising the prospect of automating board-level design tasks. However, existing agents either target chip-level design or treat datasheets as static text, offering little guidance on whether a specific component should---or even could---be used for a given board-level design. Moreover, without touching real hardware, they hallucinate incorrect details. To fill this gap, we present {\setlength{\fboxsep}{1pt}\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DS2Agent-9FE8/}{\fcolorbox{blue}{white}{DS2Agent}}}, an open-source framework that constructs interactive agents from device datasheets. Each agent comprises three models: a knowledge model supporting retrieval and question answering; a digital-twin model capturing the physical functionality of the device; and an interface model supporting driver development and system integration. To suppress hallucinations, we also allow optional connections to real devices, so that the agent can calibrate its internalized knowledge against the device. We evaluate DS2Agent on ten devices spanning seven functional categories. Compared with the baseline, the DS2Agent-augmented agent improves the question-answering score from 87 to 97 out of 100 while using 44.8\% fewer tokens. For driver generation, it reduces average token usage per device by 72.9\%. For system integration, it reduces total token usage across three FreeRTOS applications by 29.7\%.
entries.title: DS2Agent: Holistic Device Agents for Accelerated Embedded Board-Level Design

entries.abstract: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.
entries.title: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency

entries.abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).
entries.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing

entries.abstract: Language agents answer questions by searching, reading, and checking claims. A reward on the final answer says little about which of those decisions earned it, since an agent can reach the right string after redundant searches or with half the evidence missing. We treat the question as an experiment. At a saved decision point, PCCC-RL, for prefix-conditioned counterfactual credit, restores the tool state, runs the action the agent chose alongside a feasible alternative, and lets the same frozen policy finish both branches. The difference in final score then samples what the decision was worth. Replaying everything is too expensive, so the method predicts each action's credit up front, checks a random subset, and uses the recorded selection probabilities to correct the errors of that prediction, spending the budget where a further check can still move the training signal. Alternatives are drawn from the prefix alone, which keeps the comparison a usable gradient baseline. On HotpotQA and MuSiQue, joint exact match, requiring a correct answer together with complete supporting evidence, reaches 56.71% and 36.82%, gains of 4.19 and 3.86 points over a baseline with the same replay access. The gain concentrates in complete evidence chains and accumulates over many updates. Single-update effects stay uncertain, and citation coverage and scope distinctions such as "none" versus "not all" remain open.
entries.comment: 31 pages, 9 figures. Accepted at the Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML 2026)
entries.title: Learning Which Evidence-Seeking Decisions Matter: Calibrated Counterfactual Replay for Language Agents

entries.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
entries.title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models

entries.abstract: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.
entries.title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research

entries.abstract: Motivation: Testing new ideas in MRI can require substantial effort to learn sequence programming and reconstruction tools and to debug implementations before the scientific question can be addressed. Goals: Reduce the implementation and debugging burden of testing MRI ideas while retaining researcher control of scientific decisions. Approach: We developed an environment where LLM agents develop sequences in the native Siemens IDEA platform, evaluate them through Bloch simulation and reconstruction, and further iteratively refine them using scanner feedback. Results: As test cases, the agentic environment was used to implement and validate a GIRF-based gradient-calibration sequence and reconstruction in approximately 4 hours, and to develop and optimize a rapid 3-second multichannel calibration scan in approximately 12 hours of researcher-guided iteration.
entries.title: A closed-loop agentic research environment for MRI development within Siemens IDEA platform

entries.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA
entries.title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding

entries.abstract: JavaScript programs are often distributed as source code, so attackers can analyze them for vulnerabilities. LLM-based vulnerability detection agents now make this analysis much easier. To mitigate this emerging threat, we present AntiAgent, a defense that lets developers harden their programs against such detection agents. AntiAgent transforms a program before release to impede an agent's analysis. To find effective transformations, AntiAgent evolves a corpus of programs with known vulnerabilities and traces how a detection agent analyzes each evolved version. It keeps the versions on which the agent misses or misreports the vulnerability and extracts their transformations into reusable rules. To protect a new program, AntiAgent carefully divides the task between an LLM and the rules, so that the transformations adapt to the program while preserving its semantics. We evaluate AntiAgent on real-world JavaScript applications against four detection agents, including Claude Code and Codex. AntiAgent reduces the number of vulnerabilities that each agent detects by 52.0-60.7%, outperforming the conventional obfuscator JS-Obfuscator and the LLM-based transformation method FPA on every agent. The transformed programs pass all project tests, indicating that AntiAgent preserves the original program semantics. The transformation rules also remain effective on vulnerability types absent from the corpus and on programs written in another language like Python.
entries.title: Hardening JavaScript Programs against LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection

entries.abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled projector rows and noise in the vision encoder, infers the unknown scale factors, and returns most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values and accuracy to near its original level. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry, a cue that a real failure need not leave. When we round those bits away, each model answers our test questions as before, but the agent, unaided, no longer repairs either model: on LFM2-VL accuracy recovers by about 4 points, against 17 from the unrounded weights. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling. On SmolVLM the agent uses it once a sentence in the prompt, which we wrote knowing the fault, names such a statistic; on LFM2-VL, whose scale factors are larger, most sessions find the rescaled rows unaided, but none finds the noise. Swapped rows or columns, which keep the set of stored values, are not found unaided on either model within our budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.
entries.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair

entries.abstract: Learn how OpenAI built the Performance Factory, a system of Codex-powered workflows that finds and fixes performance issues to help keep ChatGPT fast.
entries.title: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

entries.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have enabled diverse retrieval methods. However, existing retrieval methods often fail to accurately retrieve results for negation and exclusion queries. To address this limitation, prior approaches rely on embedding adaptation or fine-tuning, which introduce additional computational cost and deployment complexity. We propose Direct Embedding Optimization (DEO), a training-free method for negation-aware text and multimodal retrieval. DEO decomposes queries into positive and negative components and optimizes the query embedding with a contrastive objective. Without additional training data or model updates, DEO outperforms baselines on NegConstraint, with gains of +0.0738 nDCG@10 and +0.1028 MAP@100, while improving Recall@5 by +6\% over OpenAI CLIP in multimodal retrieval. These results demonstrate the practicality of DEO for negation- and exclusion-aware retrieval in real-world settings.
entries.comment: Accepted to the RAG4Report Workshop at ACL 2026. Fixed typos and added acknowledgments
entries.title: DEO: Training-Free Direct Embedding Optimization for Negation-Aware Retrieval

entries.abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.
entries.title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering

entries.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
entries.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

entries.abstract: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.
entries.title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair

entries.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with electronic design automation (EDA) feedback is advancing large language models for hardware design and verification. Extending these gains to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span tasks, preserve state across tool calls, and support large hierarchies alongside parallel rollouts. We present SiliconGym, the first versatile, cross-task and cross-toolchain RL environment for hardware design and verification. By decoupling versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, SiliconGym scales from module-level RTL, testbench, and PPA tasks to multi-round repository repair and full-hierarchy SoC flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, finishing a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek. Using interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, we show that open-source-trained functional correctness transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation reveals when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.
entries.title: SiliconGym: A Versatile Reinforcement Learning Environment for Agentic EDA

entries.abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $π_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $π_{0.5}$.
entries.title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery

entries.abstract: Testbenches written by large language models can compile and run while leaving entire datapaths idle. We present CHORUS, the first framework to combine coverage-guided agentic reinforcement learning (RL) with policy consolidation for testbench stimulus generation. We train LLM4Cov's final supervised checkpoint to draft testbenches and repair its lowest-scoring draft using simulator feedback, raising CVDP-ECov agentic Pass@1 from 69.2% to 85.5%. Applying the same training to three checkpoints yields similar overall pass rates, yet the policies succeed on different designs. Averaging their weights combines these strengths in a single dense 4B model that reaches 86.7% agentic Pass@1. When simulator rewards select the teacher for each training prompt, the distilled 4B model reaches 88.0%, 13.5 percentage points above DeepSeek-R1 (671B).
entries.title: CHORUS: Coverage-Guided Agentic RL and Policy Consolidation for Testbench Stimulus Generation

entries.abstract: Training strong large language models (LLMs) requires high-quality supervision, which is often scarce. Recent work shows that paired preference data from weak-weaker model pairs (e.g., Qwen3 4B over 1.7B), despite the limited quality of individual responses, can provide an effective supervision signal through relative quality deltas, which we term a "weak" signal. This motivates a key research question: can multiple "weak" signals be constructively aggregated for improving strong models (e.g., Qwen3 8B)? To this end, we propose Preference Delta Aggregation (PDA), the first framework that derives a preference delta from each weak-weaker model pair, instantiates it as a LoRA adapter learned through preference optimization, and aggregates the resulting deltas via LoRA merging. To improve the composition of independently trained adapters, we introduce Geometric Alignment Merging (GAM), which aligns their left and right singular bases through orthogonal Procrustes rotations and averages the aligned factors. Evaluations on knowledge reasoning and agentic search show that PDA-GAM exceeds the strongest individual delta, with further gains along the evaluated sequences of additional deltas. Using three reasoning deltas and four agentic deltas, PDA-GAM improves Qwen3-8B by 6.8 and 7.3 points on average, respectively, exceeding the strongest single-delta baseline by 2.1 and 4.3 points. These configurations achieve the highest average scores among the evaluated merging methods, with similar gains observed on a second student model. Further analysis suggests that these gains come from composing complementary capabilities encoded across distinct preference deltas. Code is available at https://github.com/AlbertQiSun/Preference-Delta-Aggregation.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version. 39 pages
entries.title: From "Weak" Signals to Strong Models: Preference Delta Aggregation with LoRA Merging

entries.abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.
entries.title: Cyber-Physical RSI for AI-RAN: A Case Study

entries.abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.
entries.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams

entries.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.
entries.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents

entries.abstract: Collaborative perception (CP) is a promising method for safe connected and autonomous driving, which enables multiple vehicles to share sensing information to enhance perception performance. However, compared with single-vehicle perception, the openness of a CP system makes it more vulnerable to malicious attacks that can inject malicious information to mislead the perception of an ego vehicle, resulting in severe risks for safe driving. To mitigate such vulnerability, we first propose a new paradigm for malicious agent detection that effectively identifies malicious agents at the feature level without requiring verification of final perception results, significantly reducing computational overhead. Building on this paradigm, we introduce CP-GuardBench, the first comprehensive dataset provided to train and evaluate various malicious agent detection methods for CP systems. Furthermore, we develop a robust defense method called CP-Guard+, which enhances the margin between the representations of benign and malicious features through a carefully designed Dual-Centered Contrastive Loss (DCCLoss). Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on both CP-GuardBench and V2X-Sim, and demonstrate the superiority of CP-Guard+.
entries.comment: Accepted for IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing (TDSC)
entries.title: CP-Guard+: A New Paradigm for Malicious Agent Detection and Defense in Collaborative Perception

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.
entries.title: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents

entries.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
entries.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development

entries.abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.
entries.title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash

entries.abstract: Multimodal search with image-text queries helps users find notes in user-generated content (UGC) communities and serves as a key search tool for multimodal search agents. For such queries, query-note relevance depends on the user's retrieval intent and cannot be determined by visual or topical similarity alone. Simply reranking visual search results cannot fully address this challenge, as notes relevant to the user's intent may be missing from the initial candidate set. This motivates explicit intent modeling to align candidate retrieval and reranking under consistent relevance criteria. We present MMIntentFlow, an intent-driven real-time multimodal search system deployed at Xiaohongshu over an index on the order of ten billion entries. MMIntentFlow represents retrieval objectives with a hierarchical intent taxonomy and uses intent-specific relevance criteria to guide data construction, representation learning, and reranking. An offline agentic data workflow acquires candidates and verifies their relevance under these criteria to produce training supervision. The embedding model combines intent-aware contrastive learning, graded ranking, and distribution distillation, while a compact reranker assesses query-candidate evidence conditioned on predicted hierarchical intents. Evaluations demonstrate that MMIntentFlow delivers substantial gains in search engagement while supporting real-time search at industrial scale. In a user-level A/B test on the Xiaohongshu platform, MMIntentFlow outperforms the existing production system based on visual search followed by reranking, achieving relative gains of 28.17% in Top-4 query click-through rate, 18.96% in query click-through rate, and 12.56% in average time spent on search results pages per user. Production monitoring records an end-to-end P50 latency of 1.07 s.
entries.comment: 29 pages, 7 figures. Technical report. v2: Renamed IntentFlow to MMIntentFlow; technical content unchanged
entries.title: MMIntentFlow: An Intent-Driven Real-Time Multimodal Search System with Image-Text Queries at Xiaohongshu

entries.abstract: Cloud AI assistants send student data to foreign servers, conflicting with data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53, and are not grounded in the national curriculum, so they often hallucinate on local content. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but faces two costs that weight quantization does not remove. An AI tutoring session revisits the same long material every turn, so once prefix caching removes the prefill cost, decoding over a growing KV Cache dominates response time; and grounding the tutor in local knowledge by fine-tuning is too costly to repeat as that knowledge changes. We present DeepEdu-F, a framework for the Vietnamese AI tutor DeepEdu with two components. LastSet selects the critical KV Cache entries once per turn from the question's attention, decodes the whole turn from that set, and keeps the full cache so later questions can select again. REPAIR (Reliable Evidence-based Playbook Adaptation and Insight Revision) curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of updating weights. LastSet decodes up to 3.1x faster than dense decoding at a 256k-token context, faster than four sparse baselines, with accuracy close to full attention. Compared with ACE (ADD), REPAIR raises final accuracy from 70.0% to 80.5% on Formula and from 53.6% to 59.7% on FiNER, while mean task/scenario goal completion across AppWorld's normal and challenge splits increases from 9.28% to 16.28%.
entries.title: DeepEdu-F: A Framework for Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs in Vietnamese Education

entries.abstract: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.
entries.title: AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications

entries.abstract: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) offer reusable, site-specific radio priors to facilitate environment-aware network planning. However, deploying heterogeneous network nodes to meet diverse performance requirements in complex environments is challenging and requires executable workflows that coordinate scene preparation, candidate-site specification, CKM construction, optimization, and validation. This paper presents a large language model (LLM)-orchestrated agent framework for CKM-assisted network deployment optimization, where an LLM translates high-level requirements into modular, typed, and reproducible planning workflows. In this framework, an LLM layer interprets intent, selects modules, and populates normalized configurations; physics-grounded modules generate scene, CKM, optimization, and validation artifacts; and a deterministic guarded controller performs validation-guided refinement. A common target-candidate-CKM-optimizer interface supports the registration and composition of compatible planning modules, with CKM backends, samplers, and solvers remaining replaceable. We instantiate the proposed framework for base station (BS) deployment, intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) deployment, and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) trajectory planning. An urban-block case study demonstrates automatic scene consistency checks, bounded BS/IRS deployment refinement, and collision- and radio-feasible UAV planning.
entries.title: An LLM-Orchestrated Agent Framework for CKM-Assisted Network Deployment Optimization

entries.abstract: Real-time voice agents must decide when to speak, recover from disruption, and act only when the conversation requires it. But currently their evaluation is fragmented and is split across speech quality, turn-taking, tool calling, and task completion. We review 136 primary works published up to October 2, 2026, and code each on two axes: the capability an evaluation exercises, namely timing, recovery, grounded outcome, and, where relevant, multiparty conduct; and the strength of its evidence, namely evaluation conditions and grading instrument. The coding locates the gaps. Only 13 of 91 evaluation works check external state or action traces, only 5 of 21 grounded-outcome benchmarks use real human speech, and only 2 of 26 multiparty benchmarks verify state. Three claims follow. Architecture constrains deployment but does not determine results. It has been observed that benchmarks can verify outcomes, but few do. Evaluating an agent solely through one-on-one user interaction leaves critical gaps: it cannot confirm if the agent is speaking to the correct person, verify that person's authority, or identify the proper moments for strategic silence. From the taxonomy we derive TRG, short for Timing-Recovery-Grounded, a minimum reporting standard, and apply it to three published reports with different architectures. In one, tool-selection F1 is 82.5% while exact-call success is 33.0%, with no evidence of external task state. None of the three reports measures task state after an interruption. TRG governs what is reported and assigns no composite score. Per-source codes and tooling accompany the submission.
entries.comment: 23 pages including references and appendices. 136 primary works / 140 corpus artifacts (cutoff 2026-10-02); two-axis coding and TRG reporting version 2. Matching corpus release: v1.2.0, https://github.com/shivamnegi92/voice-agent-eval-corpus/releases/tag/v1.2.0. Version archive DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24288814 (record/version confirmed; download blocked for independent byte verification)
entries.title: Evaluating Real-Time Voice Agents: A Survey from Component Quality to Grounded Outcomes

entries.abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items. Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. We apply the evaluation framework to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration. Averaged over two runs per system, each scored by two LLM judges, experimental execution lags behind design and planning for every evaluated system. Within execution, systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvements. Moreover, neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably yields higher scores. ResearchFlow-Eval thus extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated, single-objective runs to continuous workflows in which systems pursue multiple claims and refine their work across iterations.
entries.title: ResearchFlow-Eval: Tracing the Execution Gap in End-to-End Multi-Claim Autoresearch

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents draw on external memory to guide new tasks, raising the question of which memories to retrieve together to improve execution. Learning set values requires outcome feedback, but evaluating each untested alternative costs an additional rollout. We introduce \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. Our analysis of how retrieval preferences limit feedback coverage motivates targeted probes. Under a correlated Gaussian surrogate, we derive a closed-form expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion that prioritizes probes by their expected benefit to local retrieval decisions. The feedback trains a shared scorer with the executor frozen, and inference requires no probing. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, \textsc{UpliftMem} achieves best or joint-best success rates among evaluated methods. On fixed-store MemSyco-Bench evaluations, decision accuracy increases from 41.7\% to 66.5\% with Qwen3-4B and from 44.4\% to 68.8\% with Qwen3-8B. At matched probe budgets, EVSI improves decision accuracy over random probing by 10.6 and 13.9 percentage points, respectively.
entries.title: UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval

entries.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://spatialagentlab.github.io/DailyBrick.github.io/).
entries.title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions

entries.abstract: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency.
