entries.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has achieved notable success in cooperative tasks, demonstrating impressive performance and scalability. However, deploying MARL agents in real-world applications presents critical safety challenges. Current safe MARL algorithms are largely based on the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) framework, which enforces constraints only on discounted cumulative costs and lacks an all-time safety assurance. Moreover, these methods often overlook the feasibility issue (the system will inevitably violate state constraints within certain regions of the constraint set), resulting in either suboptimal performance or increased constraint violations. To address these challenges, we propose a novel theoretical framework for safe MARL with $\textit{state-wise}$ constraints, where safety requirements are enforced at every state the agents visit. To resolve the feasibility issue, we leverage a control-theoretic notion of the feasible region, the controlled invariant set (CIS), characterized by the safety value function. We develop a multi-agent method for identifying CISs, ensuring convergence to a Nash equilibrium on the safety value function. By incorporating CIS identification into the learning process, we introduce a multi-agent dual policy iteration algorithm that guarantees convergence to a generalized Nash equilibrium in state-wise-constrained cooperative Markov games, achieving an optimal balance between feasibility and performance. Furthermore, for practical deployment in complex high-dimensional systems, we propose $\textit{Multi-Agent Dual Actor-Critic}$ (MADAC), a safe MARL algorithm that approximates the proposed iteration scheme within the deep RL paradigm. Empirical evaluations on safe MARL benchmarks demonstrate that MADAC consistently outperforms existing methods, delivering much higher rewards while reducing constraint violations.
entries.title: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Convergence to Generalized Nash Equilibrium

entries.abstract: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.
entries.title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation

entries.abstract: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.
entries.title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes

entries.abstract: Benchmarks for coding agents typically assess implementation from explicit specifications, leaving open whether agents can discover and reproduce systems whose rules are undocumented and accessible only through interaction. We study this capability in web games, which offer controlled environments with observable actions and outcomes, and introduce GameReplica, a benchmark for end-to-end black-box game replication. It comprises 125 instances spanning 25 web games and five core mechanism families, with each game instantiated at five difficulty levels. Under container isolation, an agent accesses the target game only through an action--screenshot interface, may iterate between probing the game, implementing a replica, and checking it, and delivers a self-contained runnable replica together with a rule checklist. A reference-grounded evaluation then scores the deliverables separately on rule consistency, implementation consistency, and visual fidelity. Experiments across six models and five agent runtimes show that black-box replication remains challenging: Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest Overall score, 71.6%, while the other models obtain 4.0%--43.0%. Every model scores highest on visual fidelity and lowest on rule consistency, suggesting that reproducing appearance is easier than recovering mechanics. Difficulty widens the gap: from L1 to L5, the four lower-scoring models show relative Overall score declines of 33%--63%, whereas the strongest model declines by less than 5%. In the evaluated configurations, outcomes vary more across models than across agent runtimes, and most attributed failures of weaker models arise during exploration, before replica code is written. Resources and interactive demonstrations are available at https://qqqqqqby.github.io/GameReplica/.
entries.title: GameReplica: A Benchmark for Black-Box Visual Game Replication by Vision-Language Agents

entries.abstract: # Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.8 ## Highlights - **Approve Python tool calls before they run.** Review the arguments and approve or reject the call. You can remember a decision for the rest of the Session. [Managed approval example](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/managed_approvals/README.md#inspect-and-decide) - **Connect your own model client.** The native tool loop works with async Responses and Chat Completions clients, LiteLLM, AnyLLM, and custom adapters. [Application-owned model clients](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/models.md#use-an-application-owned-model-client) - **Add Realtime voice to a Session.** Use a server WebSocket, connect a browser over WebRTC, or attach to an existing SIP call. [Realtime connection options](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/native_voice.md#choose-a-connection) - **Resume more kinds of work.** Save supported pending tool requests and approvals. Request and token budgets keep the usage already spent when you restore a supported checkpoint. [Restore a checkpoint with a budget](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/budgeted-recovery.md) - **Install on more Linux systems.** The preview adds an ARM64 wheel. Both Linux wheels support glibc 2.28 or newer. [Preview wheel platform requirements](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/.github/RELEASING.md#L44) ## Added - Observe tool-search calls, tool-search results, and hosted MCP approval decisions through `ModelOutputItemCompleted`. Use `include_execution_details=True` to receive full items; receive summaries by default. [Live tool observations](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/observation.py#L238-L267) - Use native Session Realtime APIs from `agents.realtime.native`, including `RealtimeAgentConfig(is_tool_enabled=...)`. Keep retained Classic/v0 Realtime imports under `agents.realtime`. [Native voice](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/native_voice.md#choose-a-connection) · [Classic imports](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/CLASSIC.md#compatible-voice-and-realtime-imports) - Handle managed function approvals with `FunctionToolApprovalRequest` and `FunctionToolApprovalDecision`. Set `run_input_policy_before_approval=True` to run the input policy before the approval predicate as well as before execution. Return `FinishTurn(output)` from `tool_batch_completion` to propose a final value with output validation and completion checks. [Managed approvals](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/managed_approvals/README.md#inspect-and-decide) · [Finish a tool batch](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/outputs.md#finish-after-a-tool-batch) - Create a remote conversation only when needed with `ConversationsHistory.ensure_conversation_id()`. Preserve a checked history prefix with `Session.replace_history_suffix(keep_prefix_count=...)`, and append staged checkpoint input with `SessionState.with_appended_pending_input()`. Read Unix milliseconds from `StoredTurn.started_at_ms` and `completed_at_ms`. [History APIs](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/reference.md#history-and-storage-apis) · [History edits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#read-and-edit-original-history) - Use `SQLAlchemySQLiteSessionStore` for an application-owned synchronous SQLite engine, and `ResponsesSocketFactoryOptions` for resolved WebSocket connection parameters. Read received logprob data through `TextLogprobsFact`, `TokenLogprob`, `TokenLogprobAlternative`, and `MalformedLogprobsFact`, with unchanged serialized record kinds. Import `ModelRunOwner` from `agents.models` and `ApplicationToolOutput` from `agents.state`. [SQLite storage](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#sqlalchemy-sqlite-storage) · [Model ownership and socket options](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/reference.md#model-run-ownership-and-websocket-options) · [Logprob facts](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-provider-logprobs) - Group prompt-cache routing for fresh Sessions with an explicit `TraceOptions.group_id`. Keep the saved cache key when restoring a Session. Set a borrowed model adapter's `prompt_cache_key` to override only that adapter's outgoing key. Treat routing as affinity without a guaranteed cache hit. [Prompt-cache routing](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/observability.md#prompt-cache-routing-for-fresh-sessions) - Route work through native handoffs or call a specialist with `Agent.as_tool()`. Add input and output guardrails, or use `Agent.decide()` for a separate typed decision with explicit input. [Handoffs](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/sessions.md#hand-off-the-conversation-to-another-agent) · [Typed decisions](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/decisions-guide.md) - Use standalone Python function tools and select MCP tools by alias. Defer eligible tool schemas with `ToolSearch`. Function tools also support strict schemas, output schemas, and an option to ignore extra arguments. [Python tool declarations](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/tools.md#python-functions) · [Tool schema discovery](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/tools.md#discover-tool-schemas) - Use Redis, MongoDB, SQLAlchemy, or a Dapr Redis state component to store supported root conversations through `CustomStorage`. Compatible Responses providers also support provider-managed conversation history. [Application-owned storage](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#store-history-in-an-application-backend) - Use ordinary manual `FunctionTool` requests and preapproved `HttpMCP` tools with `CustomStorage`. Suspend a supported manual request and restore into independent memory. To continue through the original backend, use an unchanged checkpoint with one unresolved ordinary manual call. Keep managed function approvals, pending MCP requests, and staged input outside that same-backend restore path. [CustomStorage support and checkpoint limits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#store-history-in-an-application-backend) - Open read-only execution environments, supply skills, or implement command and patch tools with application callbacks. Callbacks run with the application's permissions. [Read-only workspaces](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#inspect-a-read-only-workspace) · [Native skills](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#supply-native-skills) - Set per-request model options for sampling, retries, deadlines, and prompt caching. Request produced items and history from one-shot runs, or opt in to provider reasoning summaries and tool-argument deltas. [Model request controls](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/models.md#model-request-controls) · [Streaming and retained history](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-observations-and-retained-history) ## Changed - Native streaming HTTP can negotiate HTTP/2. Buffered Responses continue to use HTTP/1.1. - Set `NativeProvider(tool_output_token_limit=...)` to adjust the approximate tool-result budget for model context. Leave it unset to use the model's default. The setting is separate from the final answer limit. [Tool output limit reference](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/agent.py#L488-L497) ## Fixed - Reject invalid web-starter request bodies and prompts before admitting work. Reject deeply nested JSON, non-object bodies, and text without valid UTF-8 encoding. [Web-starter request validation](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/web_starter/app.py#L433-L474) - Wait for confirmed remote command exit during cancellation. Report a failure when the executor acknowledges a stop without confirming exit. - Preserve the backing store's configured history limit when a Classic compaction wrapper has no explicit settings. Explicit wrapper and per-run limits still take precedence. - Strict Python tools return a retryable error to the model when the original arguments fail validation, before approval or callback execution. A corrected call still goes through approval when required. [Function argument validation reference](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/_function_tools.py#L1390-L1404) - Preserve completed tool results during supported checkpoint restores. Report uncertain calls for reconciliation before reopening local profiles with interrupted child work. [Recover after an interruption](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#recover-after-interruption) - Preserve accepted model settings and history across supported handoffs and retries. Improve provider error reporting so applications can see where a request failed. [Inspect provider response attempts](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-response-attempts) - Harden protection for native workspace metadata and credential files. Reduce startup work for simple runs and reuse eligible HTTP connections. ## Upgrading from 0.24.0-alpha.7 - Use the alpha.8 wheel for the features in these notes. Some linked guides still refer to development builds. If an example needs files from the repository, use the revision linked in these notes. Alpha.7 does not accept newer keywords such as `strict` on `function_tool` or `model_backend` on `NativeProvider`. - For Linux local execution, install `bubblewrap` with a compatible `bwrap` in `/usr/bin` or `/bin` and allow sandbox namespace creation. For a Linux Docker executor, supply `bwrap` in the container image or executor bundle. [Linux executor setup](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#local-execution) - **Back up your saved state before upgrading.** Alpha.7 supports budgets for live runs. Alpha.8 adds checkpointing for supported pending runs with request or token budgets. The checkpoint saves the requests or tokens already used so they still count after restore. Alpha.7 rejects this new format because it cannot enforce the saved budget. We verified that both versions can reopen idle checkpoints, checkpoints waiting for a manual Python tool reply, and closed `LocalStorage` profiles on Linux x86-64. These checks used matching app settings and features available in both versions. If alpha.7 cannot reopen your saved state after rollback, restore your pre-upgrade backup. [Resume a budgeted checkpoint](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/budgeted-recovery.md) · [Checkpoint restore setup](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#supply-restore-configuration) · [Reopen a local profile](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#reopen-a-conversation-from-local-storage) - Replace bare `"*"` entries in network domain rules with exact hosts or scoped patterns such as `"*.example.org"`. To allow outbound public hosts, use `NetworkPolicy.allow_all()`. On Linux, this also requires `allow_all_unix_sockets=True` and an executor isolated from host services and other jobs. Explicit network policies remain unsupported on Windows. [Network policy and platform limits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#network-and-local-socket-access) - If you relied on a saved Codex login to enable ChatGPT Apps tools, add the existing `ChatGPTAppsMCP` declaration to the Agent's tools. Supply the provisioned Apps token, its account ID, and the tool names you want to expose. A saved Codex login now supplies model authentication only. [ChatGPT Apps setup](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/mcp.md#connect-personal-chatgpt-apps) - If your code reads `session.items()`, count each execution once. Provider `function_call` and `function_call_output` rows can accompany a typed record for the same execution. Match native `thread_id`, `turn_id`, and `call_id` rather than counting rows or relying on a history cursor's `id`. Recheck saved-history readers and analytics before upgrading. [Execution history](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-completed-execution) - If you use Classic `WorkspaceJsonlSink`, choose a log budget before upgrading. Its default is now 8 MiB. Exceeding the existing-file or pending-buffer budget drops pending events and permanently stops that sink; rebinding does not restart it. Create a new sink for a new outbox or a larger finite `max_bytes`, or use `JsonlOutboxSink` or `HttpProxySink` outside the workspace for long-lived logs. Use `max_bytes=None` only for trusted workloads that need unlimited reads. The sink does not rotate or truncate logs. [Workspace sink limits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/src/agents/classic/sandbox/session/sinks.py#L143-L186) - If you use the `classic-blaxel` extra and pin Blaxel, update the pin to `0.2.51` or newer. Test saved sandbox restoration with your current network and port settings. Blaxel, Cloudflare, Daytona, E2B, Modal, and Vercel can now reject saved settings that conflict with the current policy. Create a fresh sandbox with the required settings instead of relaxing the policy to reuse old state. [Blaxel dependency](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/pyproject.toml#L113-L117) · [Example restore-policy check](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/src/agents/classic/extensions/sandbox/blaxel/sandbox.py#L1095-L1102) ## Release verification Source: [`d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/commit/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e). Built and tested by [Tests #43800450653](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/actions/runs/43800450653). Verified fresh installs on all four platforms with CPython 3.10 and 3.14. [Installation checks](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/actions/runs/43805410415)
entries.title: Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.8

entries.abstract: Replaying a vulnerability's original proof-of-concept after patching tests whether its reported trigger remains reproducible, but does not establish that the underlying security invariant holds on other code paths. We present a benign, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study across four LLM agent frameworks and four invariant classes. For PraisonAI, we compare original-trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M). We also perform five before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI. Each run reports VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE, gated by a positive authorized control. Probes use inert markers or builtins-reachability checks. At PraisonAI 4.6.31, the original tool-loading trigger is blocked while the tool_override path still violates the invariant. This reproduces the publicly documented CVE-2026-44334 bypass of CVE-2026-40287; neither tested path shows a violation at 4.6.32. For CrewAI, we observe a violation in tested release 1.11.0 and confinement in 1.11.1, without claiming the earliest fixed release. Fourteen harness-validation scenarios produced their expected verdicts. Only one same-version B0-versus-M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probes invoke loader functions directly and establish boundary behavior under the supplied setup, not a full end-to-end exploit. A non-violation verdict applies only to the tested probe, version, and configuration and is not a proof of safety. This pilot reconstructs a known incomplete fix; it neither introduces a new testing technique nor estimates vulnerability prevalence.
entries.title: Beyond the Patch: Reconstructing an Incomplete-Fix Patch Bypass in LLM Agent Frameworks with Control-Gated, Benign Probes

entries.abstract: Spatial agents must interpret observations, maintain consistent spatial memory and make decisions over long interactions. We use Pac-Man as a testbed to study the training challenges behind these capabilities in a Qwen3.5-9B-based agent. Our research trajectory progresses from primitive-action RL on text-based mazes to visual inputs with an internal-state-assisted harness, then toward observation-driven memory and joint policy--harness improvement. The main analysis focuses on text-based maze RL; supplementary sections report visual-adaptation and harness experiments and discuss subsequent directions. Text-based maze RL requires curriculum and training-recipe design to overcome cold starts; normal-start clear rates on eight held-out mazes rise from 0% to a peak of 81.25%. In the second step, model adaptation and harness improvements raise the clear rate from 26.6% to 96.9% on one fixed map with three extra lives. These results highlight three development lessons: use curricula to address cold starts, establish visual grounding before language adaptation, and treat harness design as a determinant of agent performance. They provide practical guidance for subsequent VLM training and spatial-agent development.
entries.title: Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man

entries.abstract: Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00--45.67\%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea's Proprietary AI Foundation Model program obtain only 0.00--10.33\%. We further construct a 100-problem synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00\%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code.
entries.title: K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts

entries.abstract: We present AgentGA, a framework that evolves autonomous code-generation runs by optimizing the agent seed: the task prompt plus optional parent archives that initialize a fresh workspace. The outer loop searches over reusable starting conditions rather than editing code directly. Each generation launches a fresh autonomous run in an isolated workspace, while selected parent archives provide inherited artifacts that descendants can inspect and reuse. AgentGA couples a population-level genetic algorithm with long-horizon agents, deterministic 1:1 elite tournaments, and online operator allocation through a modified Hedge controller. We evaluate the approach for tabular AutoML on the 16-competition Weco-Kaggle Lite benchmark, including model-matched AIDE and AutoGluon comparisons. AgentGA with DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731) achieves 71.13% mean Exceeds % of Human, compared with 57.61% for model-matched AIDE and 57.89% for AutoGluon, outranking AIDE on 14/16 tasks. A control that removes inheritance, in which every agent starts from scratch, reaches 65.76% under AgentGA's stopping rule and 67.25% at the full budget, above a single long-lived agent (61.20%) and below AgentGA. These descriptive results support agent-seed optimization as a practical design choice for autonomous code-search systems, without isolating the causal contribution of inheritance.
entries.comment: 42 pages total (10-page main text + references + appendix), 11 figures, 21 tables
entries.title: AgentGA: Evolving Code Solutions in Agent-Seed Space

entries.abstract: Coding agents learn from and are measured on executable tasks, but building such tasks from repository history usually means rebuilding an environment at an old revision for every task, which is costly and brittle. We observe that a merged pull request (PR) can instead be undone on today's code: removing the effect of a bug fix or feature from a maintained revision recreates the same task inside an environment that already builds and runs. We present Change2Task, which converts merged PRs into verified tasks on an up-to-date revision of the same repository. It reconstructs the pre-change state by patch reversal, code mapping, or agent-based rewriting, and keeps a task only if its target tests pass, fail, and pass again across the healthy, task, and restored states. From 1,130 PRs spanning bug fixing, feature addition, test generation, API migration, and security repair, Change2Task builds 900 verified tasks, recovering 29% more than SWE-smith's PR Mirror on matched bug-fix candidates. The reconstructed tasks preserve the evaluation signal: in aggregate, four coding agents solve 41.1% of tasks on both the original and reconstructed versions, with 89.7% per-task agreement. Sharing modern environments across tasks further reduces setup time by 58% and storage by 71%. On 11 private industrial repositories, Change2Task yields 1,000 tasks on which the strongest model reaches only 14.6% Pass@3.
entries.comment: 27 pages, 9 figures, 9 tables, including references and appendices
entries.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments

entries.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can also induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume that memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and attempt to reduce this risk by filtering such memories at different stages of the memory pipeline. However, in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts. To this end, we propose MemAdapter, a novel framework that adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.
entries.title: Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy

entries.abstract: Collaborative edge large language model (LLM) systems often require repeated prefill computation when task contexts are transferred between agents. Reusing previously computed key--value (KV) caches can eliminate this overhead, but requires KV-cache delivery before the receiving agent begins decoding. Under strict deadlines and unreliable edge links, complete KV cache transfer may be infeasible, making the timely delivery of useful KV information critical. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that combines prioritized source transmission with adaptive loss recovery. PriorityFEC first organizes KV blocks into a utility-aware source queue to prioritize important information. It then employs ACK-sliding Streaming FEC and a lightweight Double Deep Q-Network (Double-DQN) scheduler to dynamically balance source delivery and repair transmission under deadline constraints. We implement PriorityFEC in a distributed edge LLM-serving prototype and evaluate it using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple workloads. Experimental results demonstrate that PriorityFEC preserves more useful KV information and achieves substantially higher task accuracy than competing transport schemes, particularly when the deadline is insufficient to deliver the complete KV cache.
entries.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems

entries.abstract: Enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions remains a central challenge in real-world applications. A promising solution is to treat skills as trainable states and optimize them in the same way as model parameters in neural network training. However, data-driven skill optimization is prone to overfitting to the limited trajectories collected from real environments. Overexploiting these trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved cases. This tension motivates a constrained search view of skill self-evolution, governed by an exploration--exploitation trade-off. We propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework that mitigates both risks: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration draws on prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound. Experiments across 23 model--benchmark configurations show that SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Transfer experiments further show that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/HQ-Lin/SkillBoost
entries.title: SkillBoost: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting

entries.abstract: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.
entries.title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents

entries.abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
entries.comment: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, and Zhuoshi Tong contributed equally to this work
entries.title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue

entries.abstract: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.
entries.title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers

entries.abstract: Agent harnesses decide what the model retrieves, decomposes, remembers and verifies, and most people use harnesses that are pre-built and fixed, such as Claude Code or a published memory system. Harness optimizers rewrite their own harness code rather than editing pre-built systems, and they learn from tens to hundreds of tasks, while long-horizon work offers a handful of episodes, each hundreds of tool calls long. We present Vestrum, which improves existing harnesses component by component. It reads full raw traces, states each failure as a recognizable class, and changes the one component where the error arose (a self-verification, a retrieval view, a decomposition step or a memory operation). Each change targets a failure that recurs across tasks of the same kind. Before anything runs, a generalization filter refuses changes that copy facts from the development tasks. Vestrum learns from one to ten long development episodes and improves tasks it has never seen in all five settings. On Claude Code, Vestrum raises Terminal-Bench 4 Hard from 63.7% to 70.3% of test checks at 1.03x the test cost. It raises expert cell-type agreement from 67.5% to 77.8% on held-out sections of one slide. On the GAM memory system, it raises UltraHorizon from 47.6 to 59.8, AMA-Bench from 64.2% to 74.2% and LoCoMo from 71.5% to 74.9%. It beats the GEPA prompt search we ran on the same data in every paired evaluation, and these gains hold under a test model different from the one Vestrum's search used. Across the searches, every self-verification the loop kept acts early: it checks an intermediate result against recorded evidence before the result is committed, or, on Terminal-Bench, requires an invariant and a probe before the first edit. In development, auditors that re-examined every finished answer broke more correct answers than they fixed, and the loop did not keep them.
entries.title: Vestrum: Learning the Verification, Retrieval and Structure of Agent Harnesses from a Few Long Episodes

entries.abstract: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with \texttt{grep}. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over $91$ repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.
entries.title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search

entries.abstract: Latent multi-agent communication directly transfers Key-Value (KV) cache tensors between transformer-based agents, bypassing text serialization entirely. While computationally efficient and reasoning accurate, this communication channel is opaque and vulnerable to man-in-the-middle tampering, a threat vector unaddressed by existing text-based or behavioral watermarks, which cannot operate on continuous internal representations. To address this vulnerability, we propose KVMark, a training-free, zero-bit KV-cache watermarking framework to verify inter-agent handoff integrity. Our framework introduces four core technical components: (1) position-dependent sign patterns that guarantee first-order statistical invisibility while preserving downstream attention survival; (2) per-head sign patterns with aligned detection to defeat head-averaging attacks; (3) a three-tier depth-aware strength schedule that equalizes detection sensitivity across transformer layers while maintaining invisibility against nine statistical profiling strategies; and (4) content-bound key derivation that cryptographically binds watermarks to input contexts, preventing replay attacks under Kerckhoffs's principle. Empirical evaluation on a four-agent latent pipeline demonstrates $100\%$ detection across $1{,}500$ handoffs with a $0.0\%$ false positive rate ($\text{AUROC}=1.0$), $100\%$ layer-level tamper localization ($17/17$ attacked layers identified with $0/19$ false positives), and no statistically significant reasoning accuracy degradation across four benchmarks ($N{=}300$--$500$). Furthermore, the framework enables multi-hop cascade verification to isolate compromised agents (500/500 detection at three hops), withstands adaptive white-box adversaries and the Out-of-Sight DiffMean attack (up to $α=8.0$), and generalizes seamlessly to Qwen3-8B without re-tuning (1,500/1,500 TPR).
entries.title: KVMARK: Fragile Watermarking for KV-Cache Integrity in Latent Multi-Agent Systems

entries.abstract: Agent revisions expose a fundamental correctness--efficiency trade-off during concurrent execution. Discarding ongoing work preserves latest-version correctness but wastes progress that may remain valid, whereas reusing prior work preserves efficiency but risks propagating stale state into outputs and tool effects. Existing recovery strategies resolve this trade-off in an imbalanced way with coarse-grained policies: they either favor efficiency by allowing potentially stale work to continue, or favor correctness by restarting the workflow or recomputing a linear suffix from the earliest conflict, thereby discarding unaffected progress. We present \textsc{Revise}, a validity-guided runtime for fine-grained recovery in structured agent workflows. When a revision arrives, \textsc{Revise} first intersects its delta with recorded data and control dependencies and propagates the resulting impact through the partially executed DAG to identify affected work. It then stops invalid work, preserves validity-established progress beyond the earliest conflict, and recomputes only the affected region. Incomplete provenance conservatively expands recovery, while reused results are revalidated before commit. Analysis of real coding-agent traces show online recovery opportunities: 118 sessions retain observable work before a queued later message is delivered; across 167 overlapping assistant responses, enqueue-to-completion overlap reaches 56.55~s at p95. Across 300 challenging revision/commit executions, \textsc{Revise} matches a latest-version oracle with no stale outputs or effects. On unmodified LangGraph and LLMCompiler applications using Qwen3-14B, it reduces model calls by 40.6--56.0\% relative to full restart and by 31.3--43.6\% relative to suffix recomputation. Under serving pressure, it further reduces revision-to-correct-completion tokens by 13.26\% and improves SLO goodput by 3.07--5.43\%.
entries.title: REVISE: Validity-Guided Recovery for Online Revisions in Agent Workflows

entries.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can learn domain-specific languages such as APIs and tool interfaces, enabling agents that act through standardized protocols like MCP. But LLM context windows cannot grow indefinitely, so scaling beyond individual capacity requires agent collaboration: the "Internet of Agents" (IoA). Current network stacks (OSI, TCP/IP) were designed for data delivery, not semantic coordination, so we propose two new layers: an Agent Communication Layer (L8) that standardizes message envelopes, speech-act performatives, and interaction patterns; and an Agent Semantic Layer (L9) that negotiates a shared context, grounds and disambiguates content against it, and provides consensus primitives for population-scale coordination. On two real datasets and two LLMs, L9's schema-grounded disambiguation improves accuracy on ambiguous requests by 13--72 percentage points over blind guessing, at no added cost when disambiguation is not needed; an ablation shows this gain is schema-specific for open-domain QA but not for structured slot-filling, where the protocol's round-trip structure alone already suffices.
entries.comment: To be published in the NeurIPS workshop on AgentOS
entries.title: A Layered Protocol Architecture for the Internet of Agents

entries.abstract: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, causing the swarm to aggregate on a resource and then disperse to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, rewiring the network; recruitment and exploration are thus one coupled process, and removing this coupling alone abolishes self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window--self-organized quasi-criticality--hovering near but below the critical point without settling onto a size-invariant critical state, with a finite-correlation-time activity spectrum (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f) consistent with local criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The Levy search and resource field are both least-committal: a maximum-caliber walk coupled to a maximum-entropy point process whose generic sign is clustered, with the optimal search exponent tracking the field's fractal dimension. Heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit clusters by switching agents to short local steps, binding exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.
entries.comment: 15 pages, 19 figures (7 main + 12 SI), 1 tables, Code and data: https://github.com/galenwilkerson/collective-foraging-cascades
entries.title: Self-organizing recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field

entries.abstract: Code efficiency is a fundamental aspect of software quality, yet how to use large language models (LLMs) to optimize correct programs remains challenging. Prior approaches rely on one-shot rewriting, retrieved exemplars or instructions, fine-tuning, or candidate search. In this paper, we present EffiSkill, a two-stage framework that models recurring slow-to-fast transformations as Operator Skills: persistent cards that record a transformation's intent, applicability, procedure, expected effect, and risks. Stage I distills frozen, language-specific skill libraries from slow/fast program pairs. Stage II diagnoses a new program, retrieves relevant skills, composes alternative plans, and generates up to eight candidates. These steps finish without candidate-execution feedback; public tests then filter and rank candidates, and held-out private tests determine reported correctness and speedup. Across 623 EffiBench-X tasks per language, two backbones, and separate Python and C++ evaluations, EffiSkill achieves the highest observed OPT@1 and OPT@8 among the compared methods in all four settings. Its OPT@8 margins over the strongest baselines range from 4.98 to 12.52 percentage points. These results support broader successful optimization coverage for the complete skill-guided pipeline under a shared output budget.
entries.title: Automated Code Efficiency Optimization via Agent Skill Mining

entries.abstract: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.
entries.title: TrainExplorer: Autonomous LLM Post-Training via Plan-and-Decouple Exploration

entries.abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors---memory capture and memory retention---and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.
entries.title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents

entries.abstract: Financial agents produce numerical claims that can be wrong even when their calculations execute correctly, due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions. We introduce FinVerify, an evidence-grounded framework for verifying financial agents' numerical claims. Based on an analysis of 190 incorrect trajectories from the Agent Finance Reasoning dataset, we define five error categories--temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, and financial-model fidelity--and operationalize them as verification protocols. An LLM structures claims and supporting evidence, while deterministic validators check financial requirements; when authoritative formulas are available, Z3 checks consistency with grounded inputs. FinVerify accepts only if all applicable checks pass, rejects proven violations, and abstains when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate the framework against a Direct baseline and an LLM judge across five fixed-candidate benchmarks. On Agent Finance Reasoning, accepted-claim precision increases from 56.4% for the LLM judge to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage. On XBRLFiling, FinVerify achieves 99.8% accepted-claim precision and 97.0% decision accuracy; on FinanceBench-67, it reaches 87.9% accepted-claim precision versus 69.7% for the judge. Improvements are smaller on FinQA and TAT-QA, where authoritative evidence is limited. These results suggest that explicit, evidence-backed verification can improve financial-agent reliability while exposing trade-offs between correctness, false rejection, and abstention.
entries.comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
entries.title: FinVerify: A Verification Framework for Financial Agents

entries.abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of ten agent-model configurations and 180 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 72% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only five of 30 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://asb.open-ssi.org/.
entries.title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery

entries.abstract: AI-agent networks introduce new communication demands driven by proactive interactions and autonomous task execution. Existing adaptive semantic communication schemes primarily adjust semantic representations and resource configurations within predefined processing scales and capability sets, which may be insufficient for evolving task requirements. To address this gap, we introduce elastic semantic communications (ESC), a task-driven framework that extends semantic adaptation to the runtime execution and participation of task-supporting capabilities. ESC comprises two complementary dimensions: vertical elasticity adjusts the execution intensity of existing capabilities, while horizontal elasticity reconfigures the participating capability set. The framework connects these dimensions through the expected marginal value of additional information and computation. To realize ESC, we propose an implicit-reasoning-enabled device--edge mechanism that supports variable-depth local inference through shared-parameter state updates and edge-side continuation through wireless transfer of intermediate reasoning states. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme demonstrate that the benefits of additional inference depend on wireless conditions, while task-aware edge invocation can preserve task accuracy with substantially lower state-transfer overhead.
entries.title: Implicit-Reasoning-Enabled Elastic Semantic Communications for AI-Agent Networks

entries.abstract: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.
entries.comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at IAAI-27 (AAAI 2027). 8 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
entries.title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval

entries.abstract: We present SAiFE_gym, a Python module that provides a collection of simulation environments for studying trading problems in constant product markets (CPMs) with concentrated liquidity (CL). These markets give liquidity providers (LPs) granular control over how their capital is allocated and enable them to adjust their range of liquidity provision dynamically based on market conditions, which in turn determines how they earn fees. We decompose the microstructure of CPMs with CL into interactive components that allow researchers and practitioners to capture various economic settings. We employ a vectorized approach to optimize our environments, making them scalable for high-dimensional reinforcement learning (RL) workflows, suitable for learning dynamic liquidity provision strategies. We demonstrate the benefits of our environments by evaluating the performance of RL agents in CPMs with CL under various market conditions.
entries.title: SAiFE-gym: Model-based Environments for Automated Market Making with Concentrated Liquidity

entries.abstract: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.
entries.comment: 6 pages, 0 figures. Accepted to S2AI 2026, co-located with IEEE BigData 2026
entries.title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces

entries.abstract: When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing. We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.
entries.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First

entries.abstract: Language-model agents act for people inside software, sending payments or editing records. Benchmarks such as AppWorld and WorkArena grade them with automated verifiers, whose verdicts also become reinforcement learning (RL) rewards, so a lenient verifier rewards mistakes. Verifier audits mostly hunt for runs that pass without doing the task; we ask about runs that do it and also change something nobody asked for. We mutation-test both verifiers with hand-written edits to correct runs, designed from the verifier source; an end-state check confirms each false positive. All confirmed false positives were unrequested changes; planted omissions and wrong values produced none. AppWorld's tests passed a duplicate write in all six tasks of two templates, and three RL methods that train on one of these templates would fully reward it; one count assertion per template rejected all six duplicates while passing every correct run. WorkArena's form verifier, called once after submission, passed all 36 edited runs that filled an unrequested field. Checked after every field, it caught extra fields filled first or in drop-downs but still passed all 8 runs that filled a text or reference field last. Both verifiers check that the requested change happened but not reliably that nothing else changed.
entries.comment: 24 pages. Camera-ready version, accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development". OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=uR6EWsGE48. Code and evidence: https://github.com/OpenAdaptAI/side-effect-loopholes
entries.title: Finding Side-Effect Loopholes in AppWorld and WorkArena Verifiers

entries.abstract: It is commonly understood that factoring a general $n$-bit biprime via Shor's order finding algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ gates by leveraging schoolbook integer arithmetics for addition and multiplication. Recent developments in quantum arithmetic circuits leveraging recursive Toom-Cook schemes have improved the cost scaling to $O(n^{2+ε})$. Here $ε>0$ depends on algorithm implementation details of the recursive multiplication steps, which allow for a vast number of design choices. The challenge in navigating such design space also presents an opportunity for demonstrating innovative practices in quantum software engineering in the era of open agentic science. We present a formally verified harness that ingests a design specification (namely a "policy" that describes a recursive circuit design scheme) from an external source, which may be an AI agent, and produces a set of formalized proofs covering mathematical correctness of the algorithm implementation, asymptotic scaling of the end-to-end gate cost, as well as the correctness of translating the verified algorithm to a detailed circuit implementation with an intermediate representation. The harness is published as an open challenge where human researchers and AI agents can search for more efficient factoring circuits while retaining machine-checked guarantees of correctness and end-to-end asymptotic complexity.
entries.comment: 33 pages (13 pages of main text and the rest are appendices), 8 figures. Project website: https://forshor.ai , Lean formalization: https://verifiedqc.github.io/ForShor/
entries.title: Formally verified harness for Shor's order finding algorithm with $O(n^{2+ε})$ gate cost

entries.abstract: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.
entries.title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

entries.abstract: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch a £1m partnership to help up to 25,000 young people across the UK build practical AI skills for work.
entries.title: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch £1m partnership

entries.abstract: Dots deliver launch reports unprompted, flag issues people might miss, and talk through upcoming meetings on the commute to work.
entries.title: At Holiday Extras, dots get to work before anyone asks

entries.abstract: We train a reinforcement learning agent to simplify hard unknot diagrams and pair it with a learned crossing selector to search for short unknotting sequences. Three examples found by the agent lead to an infinite family of prime two-bridge knots of unknotting number three whose connected sums with the figure-eight knot also have unknotting number three, and fifteen new unknotting upper bounds were found on the set of prime knots up to 13 crossings.
entries.title: RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number

entries.abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly used to turn natural-language requirements into code. In access control, that shortcut is dangerous: a generated policy can compile and read correctly while granting access that no one approved. The difficulty is not only writing policy code. It is fixing what the requirements mean before code is written, and then checking that the final policy actually satisfies that intent. We present AutoCedar, a verifier-guided system that first turns natural-language access-control requirements into a reviewed, checkable target, and then synthesizes Cedar policies against that target. AutoCedar decomposes schema and policy authoring into small intent atoms: reviewable claims about vocabulary and behavior. Once those atoms pass mechanical validation and human intent review, the model proposes a candidate policy, the verifier checks it against the approved target, and each failure is turned into a repair signal that tells the model whether to broaden, narrow, or restructure the policy without changing the target. Because the model's work is split into small problems, each grounded in reviewed intent and backed by verifier feedback, end-to-end policy authoring becomes tractable. AutoCedar converges on all 221 tasks of CedarBench, our benchmark of authorization tasks paired with executable semantic boundaries. Across three requirements-corpus case studies covering healthcare, education, and conference management, AutoCedar converts noisy prose and extracted access-control fragments into reviewed schemas, formal checks, and a globally verified Cedar policy store for each scenario.
entries.title: AutoCedar: An Agentic Framework for Verifier-Guided Access Control Policy Synthesis

entries.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) affects millions of US adults. Primary care-based screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment (SBIRT) is a leading strategy for identifying heavy drinking early, but access to primary care, screening, and specialty treatment differs markedly across subgroups. Whether scaling SBIRT and expanding treatment capacity narrows or widens these differences is unknown and cannot feasibly be tested in a randomized trial. We present AUDTxSim (AUD Treatment Simulation), a stochastic, spatially explicit, individual-based model of alcohol use, AUD, SBIRT, and specialty treatment for the adult populations of California and Texas. Agents represent every adult in synthetic populations of the two states (28.0 and 19.3 million adults), each geo-located to a Census tract and linked to nearby treatment facilities. In daily time steps, the model simulates: (1) annual transitions among eight alcohol use and AUD states; (2) healthcare visits, screening, brief intervention, and referral; (3) treatment seeking, standalone medication for AUD, mutual help, and requests for hospitalization, residential, or outpatient care; (4) a treatment manager that allocates individuals to facilities by preference, geography, and capacity, with telehealth substitution and waitlists; and (5) treatment progression, stepdown between levels of care, and post-treatment mutual help. It is implemented in Python with Repast4Py to run in parallel on a computing cluster. Once calibrated to state, rural-urban, and demographic targets for healthcare visits, heavy drinking and AUD prevalence, and mortality, AUDTxSim will project population-level and subgroup-specific effects of alternative SBIRT reach and treatment capacity scenarios on AUD prevalence, treatment receipt, and mortality. We report the model structure, decision logic, data sources, and calibration plan.
entries.title: Simulating access to alcohol screening, brief intervention, referral to and receipt of specialty treatment for alcohol use disorder in California and Texas: A study protocol for an agent-based modeling study (AUDTxSim)

entries.abstract: Safety filters for heterogeneous robot teams fail because of missing constraints, overestimated braking capabilities and conflicts between individually satisfiable constraints. We present OntoCBF, which compiles a domain ontology with a class taxonomy, typed relations, safety axioms and a dynamics profile per robot class into a control barrier function filter with one quadratic program per agent. Description-logic entailment supplies the constraints of any team online, including those that follow from chains of relations and from classes defined by what a robot carries, so the existing safety axioms cover new robot classes, payload classes and combinations. We prove that a subclass may reuse the braking capability of its parent whenever it can produce every velocity of the parent, a property separate from subsumption. For box-bounded double integrators this property is also necessary, and every loss of safety then begins with a conflict. Once three robots interact, the safe set of pairwise barriers contains states from which a collision is unavoidable, and such states persist in larger teams under any fixed capability reduction. In a simulated warehouse where humans ignore the robots, a filter written for the design classes violates safety in 89-100 % of the episodes with unseen classes. In all scenarios, including one with 32 robots, OntoCBF violates safety in 20-70 % of the episodes, each time after a conflict, with a median deepest intrusion of 10-17 % of the keep-out distance. A multi-agent PPO policy trained with the filter in the loop lowers the rate of infeasible quadratic programs, nearly all of them conflicts, by 18-41 %.
entries.title: Ontology-Compiled Control Barrier Functions for Heterogeneous Robot Teams

entries.abstract: Operational records from AI coding agents differ across agents, repositories, tasks, and workflows. We study 71,677 pull requests (PRs) from six agents and show that pooling these records can reverse descriptive and predictive conclusions. PRs carrying a co-authorship trailer have a 55.6% merge rate, compared with 77.5% without the trailer, but removing the dominant agent flips this -21.8 percentage-point gap to +23.7 points. We treat this Simpson-type reversal as a data-veracity problem and represent source, environment, and workflow context in a feature cascade. Gradient-boosting merge-prediction AUC increases from 0.774 to 0.832; the advantage persists under temporal evaluation (0.801) and unseen repositories (0.807). The co-authorship coefficient changes from -1.09 to +1.44 after conditioning, whereas repository-clustered AIPW intervals show no stable adjusted trailer association. A strict PR-creation-time model reaches 0.741 AUC in standard evaluation and 0.710 on unseen repositories, although its temporal AUC falls to 0.641. Finally, a separately cross-fitted analysis of an observed-mode functional estimates a +12.3-point doubly robust gain at a 30% allocation budget on the non-Codex population, only 0.5 points above risk ranking. This last result is retrospective decision support over metadata states, not a causal effect of assigning human review.
entries.title: Reliable Mining of Heterogeneous AI Coding-Agent Data: Context-Aware Prediction and Resource-Aware Ranking

entries.abstract: Tool-calling LLM agents rely on third-party skills to extend their capabilities, but this openness exposes a supply-chain attack surface in which malicious skill instructions can manipulate agent execution across multiple turns. In this work, we present Clawdrain, a Trojanized OpenClaw skill that induces resource exhaustion through a Segmented Verification Process (SVP). SVP combines stateful progression, repair-driven repetition, and termination to create costly tool-calling chains while preserving a legitimate final payload. We evaluate Clawdrain in a production-like OpenClaw deployment with real API billing across Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Clawdrain achieves 2-16 times token amplification with plain SVP, while the three models exhibit distinct behaviors, including autoregressive compliance, proactive scripting, and extended trial-and-error reasoning. Our findings reveal that agent resource exhaustion arises not only from output generation, but also from repeated context re-ingestion, tool coordination, reasoning, and recovery, motivating system-level controls over cumulative skill behavior.
entries.title: Clawdrain: Exploiting Tool-Calling Chains for Stealthy Token Exhaustion in OpenClaw Agents

entries.abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to diagnose and mitigate failures in production systems, known as agentic Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). Current SRE benchmarks are limited to oversimplistic SRE tasks and are unfortunately hard to extend due to bespoke designs. We present SREGym, a high-fidelity benchmark for SRE agents.
